Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Shopowner
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Vignette:
Marcus Heller is a 48-year-old married man of mixed North American heritage who owns and operates a small hardware and general goods store in a mid-sized Midwestern town. He presented for psychological services approximately three years after the sudden death of his adult son, Daniel, who was killed in a hit-and-run accident on a Sunday afternoon while cycling home from a friend's house. Marcus had been the one to receive the call from the hospital, and he arrived before Daniel was pronounced dead — close enough to see him on the gurney, close enough to hold his hand in the final minutes. The image of his son's face in that hospital bay, pale and still in a way Marcus had never seen, became the center of a memory that would not recede.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus moved through the expected rituals of grief — the funeral arrangements, the burial, the casseroles from neighbors — but something shifted in him that he could not name at the time. He began to notice that the memory of the hospital did not behave the way he expected a memory to behave. It did not soften or recede. Instead, it returned with a vividness that felt less like recollection and more like re-entry: the antiseptic smell, the sound of the monitor flatlining, the weight of Daniel's hand going slack. When these episodes came, Marcus was certain he was back in that room. The present moment — his shop counter, his kitchen table, his wife beside him — dissolved entirely. He had come to believe that something in his mind had broken in a way that could not be repaired, that he was condemned to relive that afternoon on a loop he could not switch off.

His store became an unexpectedly fraught environment. Customers came in carrying the ordinary texture of their lives — conversations about family, about loss, about neighbors who had died. When an elderly woman came in one autumn afternoon and mentioned, while buying weather stripping, that she had just returned from her brother's funeral, Marcus felt the film begin to play. He excused himself to the stockroom and stood among the shelving units until he could breathe steadily again. He began smoking again after eleven years without a cigarette, stepping outside to the alley behind the shop several times a day, telling himself it helped him manage the pressure in his chest. Over months, he arranged his days so that he would not pass the cemetery on the edge of town, adding seven minutes to his commute without ever explaining this to his wife. He stopped attending the memorial services and wakes that are a routine part of life in a close community, and people noticed. Invitations stopped coming. Friendships that had been maintained through shared ritual quietly contracted.

At home, Marcus had developed a vigilance that exhausted him. Unexpected sounds — a car backfiring, a door slamming in another room — produced a physical jolt that left him shaking and ashamed. His wife had learned not to enter a room without announcing herself after he spun around one evening and knocked a glass from the counter. He was certain, in the moment of startle, that something catastrophic was occurring. He carried a persistent dread — not quite fear, not quite grief, but something that combined the texture of both — and it surfaced as flashes of anger and shame that he could not always contain. He had come to believe that feeling anything too strongly was dangerous, that strong emotion was a door that, once opened, would bring the film rushing back.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a conversation with his wife, who told him quietly one evening that she felt she had lost him too. He had not cried at Daniel's grave in three years. He had not spoken his son's name in months. He arrived at the intake appointment visibly uncomfortable, smoking before he came through the door. What he said he feared most was that talking about it would make it worse — that the film would play and he would not be able to stop it. What he said he hoped for, haltingly, was to be able to remember Daniel without being destroyed by it.
